title: Git Internals
tagline: Understand Git's object model — blobs, trees, commits, and the DAG — so merges, rebases, and refs are never magic again.

sections.content:
Most developers use Git as a black box: `add`, `commit`, `push`, and pray. But Git's power — and the reason its error messages make sense once you understand them — lies in a beautifully simple **content-addressable object store**.

Every piece of data Git tracks is stored as one of four object types: **blob** (file content), **tree** (directory), **commit** (snapshot + metadata), and **tag**. Commits form a **Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)**: each commit points to its parent(s), so history is just a chain of snapshots connected by SHA-1 hashes. **Refs** (branches, tags, `HEAD`) are simply named pointers into that graph. The **staging area (index)** is a prepared snapshot waiting to become the next commit. Understanding these three ideas — object store, DAG, refs — demystifies merge conflicts, rebases, and `git reflog` entirely.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    WD["Working Directory\n(files on disk)"]
    IDX["Staging Area / Index\n(next snapshot)"]
    OBJ["Object Store\n(.git/objects)"]
    BLOB["blob\nfile content"]
    TREE["tree\ndirectory listing"]
    CMT["commit\ntree + parent + message"]
    REF["refs / HEAD\nnamed pointers"]
    WD -->|"git add"| IDX
    IDX -->|"git commit"| OBJ
    OBJ --> BLOB
    OBJ --> TREE
    OBJ --> CMT
    CMT -->|"pointed to by"| REF
sections.caption: Git's three-stage architecture: working directory → staging area → object store. Refs are lightweight pointers into the commit DAG.

sections.title: A Library with Immutable Books
sections.content:
Imagine a library where every book is given a unique catalogue number derived from its exact content — change one word and it gets a new number. That's Git's **object store**: every blob (file snapshot) and tree (directory snapshot) is hashed with SHA-1 and stored once. Identical files share the same hash — no duplication.

A **commit** is like a library catalogue entry: 'On this date, the bookshelf looked like *this* (tree), and it followed from catalogue entry *that* (parent commit).' The **DAG** is the sequence of catalogue entries over time — always forward-pointing, never cyclical.

**Branches** are sticky notes placed on a catalogue entry. When you commit, the sticky note moves forward automatically. **HEAD** is a special sticky note pointing to whichever note you are currently on. `git checkout` moves HEAD; `git commit` moves the current branch's sticky note.

**Blobs** store raw file content — no filename, no path. The same content in two directories produces one blob. This is why Git is efficient: only *changed* file contents produce new blobs.

**Trees** record the structure of a directory: a list of (mode, name, SHA-1) entries pointing to blobs (files) or other trees (sub-directories). Every commit captures the full root tree, but unchanged subtrees reuse their existing SHA-1.

**Commits** tie everything together: a pointer to a root tree, a pointer to the parent commit(s), author/committer metadata, a timestamp, and a message. Because the commit SHA-1 is derived from all of this, *any* change to history — rewriting a message, amending a commit, rebasing — produces a **new SHA-1**. History is immutable by nature.

**The DAG** means commits form a graph where edges go from child to parent. Merges create a commit with *two* parents. Rebasing replays commits onto a new base, producing new SHA-1s (even if the diff is identical).

**Refs and HEAD:** A branch (`main`, `feature/x`) is a file in `.git/refs/heads/` containing a single SHA-1. `HEAD` is a file pointing either to a branch (`ref: refs/heads/main`) or directly to a commit hash (detached HEAD). `git commit` writes a new commit, then updates the current branch file to that new SHA-1.

**Staging (the Index):** `git add` hashes the file and writes a blob to the object store, then records the blob SHA in the index. `git commit` reads the index, builds a tree, writes a commit. This is why you can `git add` partial changes — the index is your *draft* snapshot.

**Merge vs. Rebase:** A merge creates a new merge commit with two parents, preserving full history. A rebase replays commits one by one onto a target, producing a linear history but new SHA-1s. Both integrate changes; the difference is the resulting graph shape and SHA-1 stability.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A["commit A"]
    B["commit B"]
    C["commit C\nfeature"]
    M["merge commit M\n2 parents: B + C"]
    R["commit C'\nrebased onto B"]
    A --> B
    A --> C
    B --> M
    C --> M
    B --> R
    M -. "merge" .- M
    R -. "rebase" .- R
sections.caption: Merge preserves both parents (non-linear history). Rebase replays C onto B as C' (linear history, new SHA-1). Same end diff — different graph.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.code:
# ── Inspect the object store ────────────────────────────────────
git init demo && cd demo
echo 'hello git' > hello.txt
git add hello.txt

# See the blob SHA that was stored
git ls-files --stage
# 100644 8d0e41234f24b6da002d962a26c2495ea16a425f 0  hello.txt

# Inspect the blob
git cat-file -t 8d0e41  # => blob
git cat-file -p 8d0e41  # => hello git

git commit -m "initial commit"

# Inspect the commit object
git cat-file -p HEAD
# tree  <tree-sha>
# author ...
# committer ...
# initial commit

# Inspect the tree
git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree}
# 100644 blob 8d0e41...  hello.txt

# ── Refs and HEAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────
cat .git/HEAD          # ref: refs/heads/main
cat .git/refs/heads/main  # <commit-sha>

# ── Staging area tricks ─────────────────────────────────────────
echo 'line 1' > file.txt
echo 'line 2' >> file.txt
git add file.txt              # stage both lines
echo 'line 3' >> file.txt     # add another line (NOT staged yet)
git diff                      # shows unstaged line 3
git diff --cached             # shows staged lines 1-2
git commit -m "stage snapshot, not working dir"

# ── Merge vs rebase ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# Merge (preserves history)
git checkout -b feature main
git commit -m "feature work"
git checkout main
git merge feature             # creates merge commit

# Rebase (linear history, NEW sha-1s)
git checkout feature
git rebase main               # replays feature commits onto main
# Rule: only rebase local / unshared commits — never rebase shared history
sections.explanation: `git cat-file -p` lets you inspect any object by its SHA-1 prefix. The index holds staged blobs. `diff` vs `diff --cached` shows the two gaps: working-dir-vs-index and index-vs-last-commit. Rebase rewrites SHA-1s — never rebase commits already pushed to a shared remote.

sections.label: Concept
sections.code:
# ── reflog: the safety net ──────────────────────────────────────
# Every time HEAD moves, Git logs it in .git/logs/HEAD
git reflog
# HEAD@{0}: commit: add feature
# HEAD@{1}: checkout: moving from main to feature
# HEAD@{2}: commit: initial commit

# Recover a "lost" commit after bad reset:
git reset --hard HEAD~3      # oops — moved back 3 commits
git reflog                   # find the lost SHA
git checkout -b rescue <sha> # branch off the lost commit

# ── Lightweight vs annotated tags ──────────────────────────────
git tag v1.0                  # lightweight — just a ref file pointing to commit
git tag -a v1.0 -m "release" # annotated — its own object (type: tag) with tagger info
git cat-file -t v1.0          # commit (lightweight) vs tag (annotated)

# ── git stash internals ─────────────────────────────────────────
# stash creates a special commit off a refs/stash ref
git stash                     # saves working dir + index as commits
git stash list                # stash@{0}: WIP on main: abc1234 message
git stash pop                 # re-applies and drops stash@{0}

# ── Packfiles: how Git compresses storage ───────────────────────
# After many objects, Git packs them into binary packfiles:
git gc                        # triggers pack generation
ls .git/objects/pack/         # *.pack  *.idx
# Objects are delta-compressed inside packfiles — similar blobs share diffs
sections.explanation: `git reflog` is your time machine — it records every HEAD movement, including resets and rebases. Annotated tags are first-class objects; lightweight tags are just refs. `git stash` is secretly a commit. Packfiles are how Git keeps repositories compact by delta-compressing similar blobs.

sections.content: **Golden rule: SHA-1 = content address.** If two commits have the same SHA-1, they are byte-for-byte identical — history, tree, everything. If they differ, they have different SHA-1s. This means you can verify the integrity of an entire repository history with one hash. It also means `git rebase` genuinely creates *new commits* — never mutate shared history after pushing.

items: **Blobs** store raw file content by SHA-1 hash; **trees** map names to blobs/subtrees; **commits** link a tree to parent commit(s) plus metadata.
**The DAG** makes history immutable: any edit (amend, rebase) produces a new SHA-1, leaving the original untouched in the object store.
**Refs** (branches, tags) are lightweight files containing a SHA-1; **HEAD** points to the current branch or commit (detached HEAD).
**The staging area (index)** is a prepared snapshot — `git add` hashes content into the object store; `git commit` builds a tree from the index.
**Merge** creates a two-parent commit preserving full history; **rebase** replays commits for linear history — never rebase shared remote history.

quiz.question: What does a Git **blob** object store?
options: A directory listing mapping filenames to SHA-1 hashes
Raw file content, identified by SHA-1 of that content
A snapshot of the entire repository at a point in time
Metadata about the author and timestamp of a change
quiz.explanation: A blob stores raw file content only — no filename or path. The SHA-1 is derived from the content, so identical content across different files produces one shared blob.

quiz.question: What does a Git **commit** object contain?
options: A compressed tarball of all changed files
A diff patch relative to the parent commit
A pointer to a root tree, parent commit SHA(s), author info, and message
A list of staged files and their blob hashes
quiz.explanation: A commit object contains: root tree SHA, parent commit SHA(s), author, committer, timestamp, and message. It does NOT store diffs — Git computes diffs on demand by comparing trees.

quiz.question: What is `HEAD` in Git?
options: The first commit in the repository
A file pointing to the currently checked-out branch or commit
A tag marking the latest stable release
The root tree object of the latest commit
quiz.explanation: HEAD is a file in `.git/HEAD` that points to the current branch ref (e.g. `ref: refs/heads/main`) or directly to a commit SHA in detached HEAD state.

quiz.question: You run `git add file.txt` then edit `file.txt` again without a second `git add`. What does `git commit` capture?
options: The latest on-disk version of file.txt
No changes — Git sees the file is dirty and aborts
The version of file.txt that was staged with `git add`
A diff between the staged and current on-disk versions
quiz.explanation: `git commit` snapshots the index (staging area), not the working directory. The second edit is visible in `git diff` but not in `git diff --cached`, so it is excluded from the commit.

quiz.question: Why does `git rebase` produce new SHA-1 hashes even when the file changes are identical?
options: Rebase compresses blobs differently than merge
The commit object contains a new parent SHA — changing the input changes the hash
Git randomly salts SHA-1 to avoid collisions
Rebase stores diffs instead of snapshots, which changes the format
quiz.explanation: A commit's SHA-1 is derived from its content: tree, parent SHA, author, timestamp, and message. Rebase changes the parent SHA (and potentially the timestamp), so the output hash changes even if the file diff is identical.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a merge commit from a regular commit?
options: A merge commit stores a unified diff of both branches
A merge commit has two or more parent pointers
A merge commit is stored as a tag object, not a commit object
A merge commit can only be created with `git merge --squash`
quiz.explanation: A merge commit is a regular commit object with two (or more) parent SHA-1 pointers — one for each branch being merged. This is what makes the DAG non-linear at that point.

quiz.question: What is `git reflog` primarily used for?
options: Displaying the list of remote branches
Recovering commits that appear lost after a hard reset or bad rebase
Showing the diff of the last commit
Listing all tags in the repository
quiz.explanation: Reflog records every movement of HEAD locally. If you reset --hard too far or delete a branch, reflog shows the SHA-1 you were on before, letting you recover the commit.

quiz.question: Which command lets you inspect the content of any Git object by its SHA-1?
options: git show-object
git inspect
git cat-file -p
git log --objects
quiz.explanation: `git cat-file -p <sha>` pretty-prints the content of any object (blob, tree, commit, tag). `-t` prints the type. This is the primary tool for exploring Git's object store directly.

quiz.question: An annotated tag differs from a lightweight tag in that it:
options: Points to a branch instead of a commit
Is stored as its own object with tagger name, date, and message
Cannot be pushed to a remote
Automatically triggers a CI pipeline
quiz.explanation: An annotated tag (`git tag -a`) creates a `tag` object in the object store with its own SHA-1, containing the tagger, date, and message. A lightweight tag is just a ref file pointing directly to a commit.

quiz.question: Which statement about Git packfiles is correct?
options: Packfiles store only the latest version of each file to save space
Packfiles delta-compress similar objects, storing only differences between similar blobs
Packfiles replace the object store entirely and disable `git cat-file`
Packfiles are created on every `git commit` automatically
quiz.explanation: Packfiles delta-compress similar blobs (e.g. successive versions of the same file) so only the delta is stored, not full copies. They are created by `git gc` or during fetch/push operations, not on every commit.
